terms.definition: The whole process of breaking food down into pieces and nutrients small enough for the body to absorb and use.
terms.function: Converts food into nutrients cells can use for energy, growth, and repair, and packages up whatever the body can't use for elimination.
terms.whereItIs: Runs the length of the digestive tract, from the mouth to the rectum.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the only way anything you eat actually becomes usable fuel and building material for your cells.

terms.definition: The entry point of the digestive tract, where teeth and tongue physically break food apart and saliva starts breaking it down chemically.
terms.function: Teeth and tongue mechanically break food into smaller pieces while saliva's enzyme (amylase) begins chemical breakdown of starches, forming a soft mass called a bolus.
terms.whereItIs: The very top of the digestive tract, just above where the esophagus begins.
terms.whyItMatters: Breaking food into smaller pieces here gives every later station a head start — a chunk that's already partly broken down digests faster and more completely.

terms.definition: A J-shaped muscular pouch that churns food and bathes it in strong acid and enzymes.
terms.function: Churns food and bathes it in hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin, breaking proteins down into a semi-liquid mixture called chyme.
terms.whereItIs: Upper-left part of the abdomen, just below the esophagus, on the widest curve of the digestive tract.
terms.whyItMatters: The stomach's acid doesn't just help digest protein — it also kills most of the bacteria that come in with food, protecting the rest of the digestive tract.

terms.definition: A long, coiled tube (about 6-7 meters folded up) where most digestion finishes and nutrients pass into the bloodstream.
terms.function: Bile, pancreatic enzymes, and villi-lined walls complete digestion and absorb nutrients into the bloodstream.
terms.whereItIs: Filling the lower-central part of the abdomen, coiled compactly.
terms.whyItMatters: This is where digestion actually pays off — its villi-covered walls create a huge surface area, so this one organ absorbs the vast majority of the nutrients your body gets from food.

terms.definition: A thicker tube that frames the small intestine on three sides and reclaims water from digested material.
terms.function: Frames the small intestine (ascending, transverse, descending colon) and absorbs water and remaining salts, compacting leftover material into solid waste.
terms.whereItIs: Wrapping around the outer edge of the small intestine's coils — up the right side, across the top, and down the left side of the abdomen.
terms.whyItMatters: Without the large intestine reclaiming water here, your body would lose far too much fluid every time you had a bowel movement.

terms.definition: The rectum and anal canal, where the digestive tract's leftover material is stored and released.
terms.function: The rectum stores compacted waste until the anal sphincter releases it from the body as stool, completing the digestive process.
terms.whereItIs: The very bottom of the digestive tract, below the large intestine's final curve.
terms.whyItMatters: This final step is what lets your body get rid of everything it couldn't use — without it, waste would build up with no room left for new food to be processed.

terms.definition: Physically breaking food into smaller pieces, like chewing with teeth or churning in the stomach.
terms.function: Increases food's exposed surface area so chemical digestion (enzymes and acid) can work on it faster.
terms.whereItIs: Happens mainly in the mouth (chewing) and stomach (churning).
terms.whyItMatters: Without this physical breakdown first, chemical digestion alone would take far longer to process a meal.

terms.definition: Breaking food's molecules apart using acids and enzymes, turning large molecules into small ones the body can absorb.
terms.function: Uses enzymes and stomach acid to break carbohydrates, proteins, and fats down into absorbable building blocks.
terms.whereItIs: Begins in the mouth with saliva, continues in the stomach with acid and pepsin, and finishes in the small intestine with bile and pancreatic enzymes.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the step that actually makes nutrients small enough to cross into the bloodstream — mechanical breakdown alone can't do that.

terms.definition: A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction, such as breaking a big food molecule into smaller pieces, without being used up itself.
terms.function: Speeds up the chemical breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats at multiple stations along the digestive tract.
terms.whereItIs: Released in saliva (mouth), stomach fluid (stomach), and bile/pancreatic fluid delivered into the small intestine.
terms.whyItMatters: Without enzymes, chemical digestion would happen far too slowly to keep up with how often the body needs fuel.

terms.definition: Tiny finger-shaped folds lining the small intestine that increase its surface area so more nutrients can be absorbed into the blood.
terms.function: Multiply the small intestine's inner surface area, giving nutrients vastly more contact points to pass into the bloodstream.
terms.whereItIs: Covering the inner wall of the small intestine.
terms.whyItMatters: Villi are the main reason the small intestine, not the stomach, absorbs most of the body's nutrients.

terms.definition: Wave-like muscle squeezes that push food along the digestive tract, from the esophagus all the way to the end.
terms.function: Moves food and digested material forward through the digestive tract regardless of body position.
terms.whereItIs: Occurs along the entire length of the digestive tract, from the esophagus through the intestines.
terms.whyItMatters: It's why food keeps moving through your system even when you're lying down — digestion doesn't depend on gravity.

terms.definition: The process of nutrients passing from inside the digestive tract into the bloodstream.
terms.function: Transfers digested nutrients (and, in the large intestine, water) across the digestive tract's lining and into the blood.
terms.whereItIs: Happens mainly in the small intestine (nutrients) and large intestine (water).
terms.whyItMatters: Absorption is the actual handoff point where digestion's work becomes usable fuel for the rest of the body.

terms.definition: A substance from food, like protein, carbohydrate, fat, vitamin, or mineral, that the body needs to work and grow.
terms.function: Supplies the energy and building materials every cell in the body needs to function, grow, and repair itself.
terms.whereItIs: Extracted from food throughout digestion, then absorbed into the blood mainly in the small intestine.
terms.whyItMatters: Nutrients are the entire reason the body digests food in the first place.
